instructions: Heat the broiler to high with a rack about 6 inches below it. Take the goat cheese out of the fridge so it softens a little.
Drain the peppers and pat them dry with paper towels. You should have about 12.
Gently open the stem end of each pepper with your finger, taking care not to tear it.
Fill each pepper with about 2 tsp of the goat cheese, using a small spoon. Press it in so the pepper is full but still holds its shape.
Lay the peppers in a single layer in a metal baking pan or an oven-safe ceramic dish.
Finely chop the garlic. Drizzle 1 tbsp of the olive oil over the peppers, then scatter over the garlic, 1/8 tsp salt and 1/8 tsp pepper.
Slice the baguette, lay the slices on a baking sheet and drizzle them with the last 1 tbsp olive oil.
Broil the bread for 1 to 2 minutes, until it's golden at the edges. Watch it closely. It burns fast. Set it aside.
Broil the peppers for 7 to 10 minutes, until the cheese is soft and bubbling at the openings.
Meanwhile, chop 2 tbsp of the parsley leaves.
Scatter the parsley over the peppers and serve warm with the toasted baguette.
method_notes: All three versions fill whole jarred piquillo peppers with a soft or sliced cheese and warm them until the cheese softens, served as a tapa. Food.com (the lead) fills them with goat cheese, drizzles them with olive oil and garlic and broils them until bubbling; Cookipedia slips in slices of tetilla seasoned with oregano and pimentón and pan-fries them briefly, and Show Me the Yummy mixes goat cheese with manchego and bakes the peppers to serve on toasted bread. This follows the lead with a fuller filling, about 2 tsp per pepper, plus a parsley finish from Cookipedia and toasted baguette alongside. No version read had a rating and RecipeTin Eats (the trusted cook for Spanish) has no version, so this leads with Food.com's, the closest to the usual tapa.
